subtopic: Producer / Consumer relation and fusion boundary
learningObjective: Explain when a producer-consumer relation between two ops in a tensor IR permits fusion into a single kernel and when it does not.
stem: Two ops form a producer-consumer relation: op P produces tensor `t`, op C consumes `t`. Which condition is generally required for fusing P and C into a single kernel that avoids materializing `t` in memory?

options.text: P and C must be implemented in the same source language (e.g., both C++ or both Triton); mixed-language producer/consumer pairs cannot be fused because their calling conventions differ. In this reading, cross-language producer-consumer fusion (say a CUDA C++ producer feeding a Triton consumer) is fundamentally impossible because their calling conventions differ, and the compiler must materialize the intermediate tensor between them.

Each element of `t` consumed by C must be producible on demand at C's iteration site; equivalently, P's per-element production and C's per-element consumption must share (or be tileable into) a common iteration space.

P and C must have the same op name (e.g., two `add` ops), because fusion in tensor compilers works by op-name pattern matching only. Under this framing, fusion in tensor compilers is implemented purely by textual pattern matching on op names; the scheduler looks up pairs like `(add, add)` or `(mul, add)` in a table and applies fusion iff both ops match a registered pair.

P must be marked as a `pure` op and C as a `side-effecting` op; only pure-into-side-effecting fusion pairs are legal because the intermediate value would otherwise persist in memory. Under this account, only pairs where the producer is annotated `pure` and the consumer is annotated `side-effecting` can fuse; matching-polarity pairs (both pure) cannot fuse because the intermediate would otherwise leak into globally-visible memory.

explanation: Fusing P and C into a single kernel that avoids materializing `t` requires that each consumed element of `t` can be produced at the moment C needs it, without global synchronization. This is expressed as sharing (or being tileable into) a common iteration space: pointwise-into-pointwise is the classic case (identical elementwise iteration); pointwise-into-reduction fits when the reduction consumes each producer element once. Cases where the consumer needs values C's iteration cannot see (e.g., all-to-all shuffles) do not fuse this way. Source language, op names, and side-effect polarity are not the governing conditions.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: language identity is a codegen concern, not a semantic fusion condition.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: shared/tileable iteration space is the core condition for producer-consumer fusion.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: fusion is data-dependence based, not op-name based.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: side-effect polarity is not the condition; both being pure is typically preferred, not opposite polarity.

assumptions: P and C both operate on tensor values with well-defined per-element production/consumption.
The compiler has an iteration model at some IR level (loop-form or structured tensor form).
nonImplications: Does not imply that every producer-consumer pair with a shared iteration space is worth fusing; register pressure and code size are additional heuristics.
Does not imply reductions can never fuse; matching consumer/producer patterns for reductions is well-known (softmax epilogue, etc.).

distractorRationales.A: Wrong sufficiency claim on language identity.
